analysis.one_liner: Guarantees workers their jobs back after leave for childbirth, family illness, or schooling, with an employer tax break.
analysis.headline: The bill never came to a vote: introduced October 1, 1991, it sat in two House committees and a subcommittee until the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have given workers who left a job for childbirth, adoption, a serious illness of their own or a close family member, or up to a year of education the right to get their job, or an equivalent one, back afterward. It covered workers with at least 2,000 hours of service in the prior 14 months, let employers deny reinstatement to their highest-paid 10% of workers, and offset employer costs with a new tax deduction for half the cost of wages and benefits paid during leave. It never advanced beyond committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers long-tenured enough to qualify (2,000 hours in the prior 14 months) who needed to step away from a job for the birth or adoption of a child, to care for a newborn or new child for up to six years, to care for a family member with a serious health condition for up to two years, or to enroll in an education program for up to a year. The bill guaranteed their old or an equivalent position back, with benefits accrued before the leave preserved, and gave them Labor Department and court remedies if an employer refused.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Long-tenured workers taking family, medical, or education leave

how_it_helps.text: An eligible worker who left for a legitimate personal purpose had to be restored to the original or a similar position, or notified when one became available within a year of applying for reemployment.

Qualifying purposes included pre-birth leave, up to six years after a birth or adoption or foster placement to care for the child, up to two years to care for a family member with a serious health condition, and up to one year for education.
Workers could enforce the right through Labor Department charges and federal court actions, with courts able to order back wages and benefits and attorney's fees to the prevailing party.
The bill extended the same rights to employees of Congressional agencies and the House of Representatives.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would have to hold positions open or reinstate returning workers, comply with notice rules, and face court-ordered back pay if they failed; the Treasury, which would forgo revenue from the new deduction equal to 50% of wages and benefits paid during qualifying leave; and the Labor Department, which would have to administer an enforcement process.

drawbacks.text: The bill guaranteed a job back, not pay during leave: a worker got nothing unless the employer's own plan paid, and eligibility required exhausting all sick, annual, and vacation leave first, so workers without savings might be unable to use the right at all.

The reemployment right could be waived in a written agreement with the employer, and the highest-paid 10% (or top five) of employees at a facility could be denied reinstatement if the employer claimed substantial and grievous economic harm.

Employers argued that guaranteeing reinstatement after absences of up to six years, and paying a new 50% tax deduction on top of it, imposed real costs and uncertainty on staffing, particularly for smaller operations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core promise was real: a returning parent or caregiver would get an equivalent job back with accrued benefits preserved, backed by court enforcement. But the design was weaker than it first appears because the leave was unpaid and required burning through all existing leave first, the longest entitlements (up to six years of parental leave) were hedged with employer exemptions and waivers, and the tax deduction mainly rewarded employers who already provided paid leave. On balance it was a meaningful job-security gain for established workers, at a modest and partly subsidized cost to employers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Education and Labor and Ways and Means committees on the day it was introduced, forwarded to the Labor-Management Relations subcommittee three weeks later, and never came back out; it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Bilirakis introduced the bill on October 1, 1991, with one Republican cosponsor.
It was referred jointly to the House Committees on Education and Labor and on Ways and Means the same day.
On October 24, 1991, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations, and the action record shows no markup, committee vote, or floor action for the rest of the 102nd Congress.
The Congress ended on January 3, 1993, so the bill expired without ever receiving a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers were better off: no reemployment mandate, notice obligations, litigation exposure, or new leave-related tax rules ever took effect, and workers who needed to step away from a job for childbirth, caregiving, or education remained without a federal guarantee of getting their position back.

for.name: Rep. Michael Bilirakis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and chose an incentive-plus-mandate design: a reemployment guarantee paired with a 50% tax deduction for employer leave costs.

against.name: Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on October 24, 1991 and took no further action on it.

against.name: William Ford
against.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the referral and never scheduled a markup or committee vote on the bill before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken. The bill had a single Republican sponsor and one Republican cosponsor [S4], in a Congress where the competing family-leave fight split largely by party, but this bill itself never drew a recorded division.

industries.note: The bill would have required them to reinstate workers who took long family, medical, or education leave and exposed them to lawsuits for back pay, while the 50% tax deduction would have subsidized the wages and benefits paid during such leave. Its death left employers with no new obligation.

The bill created a new deduction for 50% of leave-related wages and benefits, reducing federal revenue, though the deduction was designed to encourage employers to offer paid leave rather than simply enrich shareholders.
